Chapter overview

Nineteenth-century Tamil socio-political change moved from colonial education and religious response to women’s reform debates, anti-caste organisation, linguistic consciousness, manuscript recovery and formal community representation.

Colonial transitionReligious & social reformTamil renaissanceAnti-caste organisationPolitical representation
Scope, Historical Context and Sources

Nineteenth-century Tamil socio-political life was reshaped by colonial administration, printing, education, missionary activity, caste conflict, religious reform, linguistic research and new forms of organised representation.

Historical Context

By the beginning of the nineteenth century, British authority had become firmly established across most of the Tamil region.

Colonial rule introduced major changes in:

  • Land-revenue administration
  • Law and courts
  • Education
  • Printing
  • Missionary activity
  • Employment
  • Language studies
  • Public communication

British officials and Christian missionaries frequently described Indian society as backward or superstitious. This created different responses among Tamil intellectuals and communities.

Some reformers:

  • Accepted selected elements of Western education
  • Criticised caste and social inequality
  • Reinterpreted religious traditions
  • Defended Tamil language and culture
  • Established schools and associations
  • Used printing to reach wider audiences

Others opposed both colonial cultural domination and local caste oppression.

Meaning of Socio-Political Movement

A socio-political movement attempts to change:

  • Social relationships
  • Access to education
  • Caste status
  • Religious practices
  • Gender relations
  • Civil rights
  • Public representation
  • Political authority

Nineteenth-century Tamil movements were not all identical.

They included:

  • Religious reform
  • Religious revival
  • Anti-caste assertion
  • Women’s rights struggles
  • Linguistic research
  • Cultural renaissance
  • Community organisation
Main Historical Phases
Early Nineteenth Century
  • Expansion of missionary education
  • Growth of printing
  • Ayya Vaikundar’s movement
  • Beginning of the Upper Cloth agitation
Mid-Nineteenth Century
  • Veda Samaj
  • Vallalar’s Sanmarga movement
  • Saiva revival
  • Linguistic research by Caldwell
  • Widow-remarriage and women’s-education debates
Late Nineteenth Century
  • Theosophical Society at Adyar
  • Ramakrishna movement in Madras
  • Tamil manuscript recovery
  • Iyothee Thass’s anti-caste organisations
  • Rettamalai Srinivasan’s community mobilisation
  • Emergence of print-based social politics
Sources

Important sources include:

  • Government records
  • Missionary reports
  • Census reports
  • Newspapers
  • Journals
  • Pamphlets
  • Religious texts
  • Association proceedings
  • Personal writings
  • Court records
  • Colonial ethnographic accounts
  • Oral traditions

Missionary and colonial records may exaggerate their own reforming role. Community traditions may present reformers through sacred or heroic narratives. Both require careful comparison.

Colonial Intervention, Printing and Modern Education

Printing and modern education expanded literacy and public debate, but they also served missionary and colonial purposes; Tamil reformers adapted the same tools for social criticism and cultural defence.

Printing in Tamil

Tamil printing began before the nineteenth century, but it expanded greatly during the colonial period.

Important landmarks:

  • 1578 — Thambiran Vanakkam was printed at Goa.
  • 1709 — Bartholomäus Ziegenbalg established a full-fledged press at Tranquebar.
  • 1812 — Thirukkural was among the early classical Tamil works to be printed.

The nineteenth century saw the gradual transition from:

  • Palm-leaf manuscripts
  • Handwritten copies
  • Restricted scholarly circulation

to:

  • Printed books
  • School textbooks
  • Newspapers
  • Journals
  • Religious pamphlets
  • Public political literature

Printing enabled the same text to reach readers across different towns and social groups.

Missionary Activity

Christian missionaries established:

  • Schools
  • Printing presses
  • Teacher-training centres
  • Translation projects
  • Girls’ schools
  • Institutions for socially marginalised communities

Missionaries produced:

  • Tamil grammars
  • Dictionaries
  • Translations
  • Prose textbooks
  • Religious tracts

Missionary schools made literacy available to some communities that had faced exclusion from traditional education.

However, missionary activity also had a conversion objective and often portrayed Tamil religious practices as inferior. This encouraged Hindu and Saiva scholars to establish their own schools and presses.

Modern Education

Colonial and missionary education introduced:

  • English
  • Modern science
  • Geography
  • History
  • Mathematics
  • New administrative skills
  • Printed examinations
  • Certificate-based education

Education created a new group of:

  • Teachers
  • Clerks
  • Lawyers
  • Journalists
  • Doctors
  • Government employees

This educated public later formed:

  • Social-reform associations
  • Community organisations
  • Political bodies
  • Newspapers
Social Effects

Printing and education helped people debate:

  • Caste
  • Women’s rights
  • Child marriage
  • Widowhood
  • Religious authority
  • Language
  • Social equality
  • Political representation

Printing therefore became both:

  • An instrument of colonial and missionary influence
  • A tool used by Tamil reformers to challenge colonialism and caste hierarchy.
Women’s Education, Widow Remarriage and Reform Debates

Women’s education, widow remarriage and age-of-consent debates exposed the tension between legal reform, social custom, caste authority and colonial intervention.

Position of Women

Women’s social position differed according to:

  • Caste
  • Community
  • Class
  • Region
  • Family status

Common concerns raised during the nineteenth century included:

  • Child marriage
  • Denial of education
  • Enforced widowhood
  • Restrictions on remarriage
  • Limited property rights
  • Dress restrictions
  • Lack of access to public institutions
Women’s Education

Missionaries and reform associations opened schools for girls.

Early opposition arose from fears that education would:

  • Weaken family authority
  • Encourage religious conversion
  • Challenge caste customs
  • Make women reject traditional roles

Supporters argued that education would improve:

  • Literacy
  • Health
  • Family welfare
  • Economic independence
  • Public participation
Widow Remarriage

The Hindu Widows’ Remarriage Act was enacted in 1856 following reform campaigns led prominently by Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar.

Although it applied throughout British India, social acceptance remained limited in many regions.

Widow remarriage was opposed particularly within communities that associated widowhood with:

  • Ritual purity
  • Family honour
  • Property control
  • Caste status

Reform organisations such as the Veda Samaj supported widow remarriage.

Age-of-Consent Debate

Colonial legislation attempted to regulate the minimum age for marital sexual relations.

Important stages included:

  • 1860 — the age was fixed at ten.
  • 1891 — it was raised to twelve.

The legislation created debate between:

  • Reformers seeking protection for girls
  • Conservatives opposing colonial intervention in personal law

Legal reform did not automatically end child marriage because enforcement and social awareness remained weak.

Relationship to Later Chapters

This nineteenth-century debate created the foundation for later campaigns led by:

  • Women’s organisations
  • Muthulakshmi Reddy
  • Self-Respect activists
  • Dravidian reformers

Detailed twentieth-century marriage, women’s-rights and Devadasi legislation belongs to Chapters 21–29.

Veda Samaj and Reformist Currents in Madras

The Veda Samaj represented an urban reformist current influenced by the Brahmo Samaj, combining monotheism with selected social reforms.

Foundation

The Veda Samaj was established in Madras in 1864.

Its emergence followed the visit and lectures of:

  • Keshab Chandra Sen

An important organiser was:

  • K. Sridharalu Naidu

The movement was influenced by the Brahmo Samaj.

Religious Principles

The Veda Samaj promoted:

  • Belief in one God
  • Opposition to meaningless rituals
  • Criticism of superstition
  • Simplification of worship
  • Ethical religious life

Its members attempted to separate religion from elaborate caste-based ceremonies.

Social Reforms

The Veda Samaj supported:

  • Women’s education
  • Widow remarriage
  • Reduction of caste distinctions
  • Inter-caste social interaction
  • Reform of marriage customs
  • Reform of funeral practices
Sridharalu Naidu

K. Sridharalu Naidu:

  • Studied the Brahmo Samaj movement
  • Translated reformist religious works into Tamil and Telugu
  • Conducted preaching tours
  • Helped spread the movement in South India

The organisation was later associated with the name:

  • Brahmo Samaj of Southern India
Importance

The Veda Samaj represented a reformist response from within educated Hindu society.

It differed from:

  • Vallalar’s compassion-centred spiritual movement
  • Vaikundar’s mass anti-caste religious movement
  • Iyothee Thass’s rejection of Hindu caste identity

Its social base remained mainly urban and educated, and it did not become a large mass movement.

Theosophical Society and Ramakrishna Movement

The Theosophical Society and Ramakrishna movement renewed interest in Asian religions through different methods: comparative universalism on one side and Vedanta-centred service on the other.

Theosophical Society

The Theosophical Society was founded in New York in 1875.

Its important early leaders included:

  • Helena Petrovna Blavatsky
  • Henry Steel Olcott

Its international headquarters was established at:

  • Adyar, Madras
  • In 1882
Main Objectives

The Society promoted:

  • Universal brotherhood
  • Comparative study of religions
  • Study of philosophy and science
  • Interest in Asian religious traditions
  • Opposition to racial superiority

Its work encouraged educated Indians to reassess religious traditions that colonial writers had dismissed as inferior.

Henry Steel Olcott

Olcott became associated with:

  • Buddhist revival
  • Education
  • Theosophical organisation
  • Schools for disadvantaged communities

His later contact with Iyothee Thass became important in the Tamil Buddhist revival.

Annie Besant

Annie Besant later became a major leader of the Society.

Her detailed contributions to:

  • Home Rule
  • Women’s organisations
  • Nationalist politics

belong to Chapters 17 and 19.

Ramakrishna Movement

Swami Vivekananda founded the Ramakrishna Mission in 1897.

The Ramakrishna Math in Madras was established in March 1897 by:

  • Swami Ramakrishnananda

Its first location was:

  • Castle Kernan
  • Commonly called the Ice House
  • Later known as Vivekanandar Illam
Activities

The Ramakrishna movement promoted:

  • Vedanta
  • Religious harmony
  • Service to humanity
  • Education
  • Healthcare
  • Relief work
  • Spiritual discipline
Historical Distinction

The Theosophical Society sought a universal comparative understanding of religions.

The Ramakrishna movement presented service and Vedanta as means of religious and social renewal.

Neither should be confused with the direct anti-caste programmes of Vaikundar, Vallalar or Iyothee Thass.

Upper Cloth Movement and Nadar Social Assertion

The Upper Cloth Movement converted clothing into a struggle over bodily autonomy, caste dignity and women’s public status in South Travancore.

Background

In nineteenth-century South Travancore, caste regulations controlled:

  • Clothing
  • Ornaments
  • Housing
  • Access to roads
  • Access to public institutions
  • Forms of bodily behaviour

Women belonging to socially subordinated communities, especially Nadar women, were prevented from wearing upper garments in the manner permitted to dominant-caste women.

South Travancore included areas now situated in:

  • Kanyakumari district
  • Southern Kerala
Beginning of the Agitation

Christian Nadar women who attended missionary churches began wearing:

  • Jackets
  • Upper cloths
  • New forms of clothing associated with conversion and education

Dominant groups treated this as a challenge to caste status.

The agitation developed through:

  • Petitions
  • Refusal to obey dress restrictions
  • Missionary representations
  • Public confrontation
  • Violence against women
  • Destruction of houses, schools and churches

The major struggle continued from the early nineteenth century until 1859.

Proclamations

Different Travancore proclamations alternately granted and restricted clothing rights.

A major proclamation was issued on:

  • 26 July 1859

It permitted Nadar women to cover their upper bodies, although discriminatory restrictions on imitating dominant-caste styles remained.

Nature of the Movement

The struggle concerned more than clothing.

Upper-body covering represented:

  • Human dignity
  • Bodily autonomy
  • Rejection of caste inferiority
  • Women’s rights
  • Public social status
Nadar Social Mobility

Missionary education and new economic opportunities helped some Nadars develop:

  • Literacy
  • Organisational networks
  • Commercial mobility
  • Community consciousness

Later Nadar associations belong mainly to Chapter 21 because major organised bodies developed during the twentieth century.

Exam Caution

The movement is known by several names:

  • Upper Cloth Movement
  • Upper Cloth Revolt
  • Channar Revolt
  • Channar Lahala
  • Marumarakkal Samaram

It occurred in Travancore, not directly under the ordinary administration of the Madras Presidency. However, much of its Tamil-speaking region later became part of Tamil Nadu.

Ayya Vaikundar and the Ayyavazhi Movement

Ayya Vaikundar combined religious teaching, anti-caste mobilisation, social dignity and political criticism through the Ayyavazhi movement.

Early Life

Ayya Vaikundar lived from:

  • 1809 to 1851

He was born at:

  • Sasthankoilvilai
  • Present-day Samithoppu near Kanyakumari

His original name is traditionally given as:

  • Mudichudum Perumal

It was changed to:

  • Muthukutty

The change is associated with caste objections to the original royal-sounding name.

Social Conditions

Vaikundar worked in the context of severe caste restrictions in South Travancore.

Oppressed communities faced limitations concerning:

  • Clothing
  • Headgear
  • Temple access
  • Public roads
  • Education
  • Social dignity
  • Taxation
  • Religious practices
Teachings

Vaikundar preached:

  • Human equality
  • Abolition of caste differences
  • Social unity
  • Rejection of unnecessary rituals
  • Opposition to animal sacrifice
  • Dignity for oppressed communities
  • Criticism of unjust political authority

He criticised:

  • British authority
  • The caste-based rule of Travancore
Samithoppu

In 1833, Vaikundar began a period of meditation at Samithoppu.

Samithoppu became:

  • His principal centre
  • A place of worship
  • A centre of social organisation
Samathuva Samajam

Vaikundar founded the:

  • Samathuva Samajam

Its practices included:

  • Inter-dining
  • Collective worship
  • Unity across caste divisions
  • Shared social identity

He encouraged followers to wear the turban as a symbol of:

  • Honour
  • Dignity
  • Self-respect
Imprisonment

The Travancore government imprisoned Vaikundar because his activities challenged established political and social authority.

Ayyavazhi

His followers called him:

  • Ayya

The movement became known as:

  • Ayyavazhi
  • The Path of Ayya

His teachings are principally preserved in:

  • Akilathirattu Ammanai
  • Ayyavazhi religious tradition
Importance

Vaikundar combined:

  • Religious reform
  • Anti-caste mobilisation
  • Social dignity
  • Political criticism
  • Community organisation

He should not be described merely as a religious preacher. His movement had a strong social-protest dimension.

Vallalar and Samarasa Suddha Sanmarga

Vallalar centred reform on Jeevakarunyam, feeding the hungry, non-killing, equality and worship of divine light rather than caste-bound ritual.

Early Life

Ramalinga Adigal lived from:

  • 1823 to 1874

He is popularly known as:

  • Vallalar
  • Ramalinga Swamigal
  • Arutprakasa Vallalar

He was born at:

  • Marudhur near Chidambaram

After his father’s death, his family moved to Madras.

Jeevakarunyam

The central principle of Vallalar’s teaching was:

  • Jeevakarunyam
  • Compassion towards all living beings

It required:

  • Feeding the hungry
  • Non-killing
  • Avoidance of meat
  • Mercy towards animals
  • Compassion beyond caste and religion

Vallalar treated hunger as a fundamental moral and social problem.

Sanmarga Organisation

He established the:

  • Samarasa Vedha Sanmarga Sangam in 1865

It later became known as:

  • Samarasa Suddha Sanmarga Sathya Sangam

Its ideals included:

  • Universal brotherhood
  • Equality
  • Compassion
  • Rejection of caste barriers
  • Opposition to empty ritual
  • Worship of divine light
Sathya Dharma Salai

In 1867, Vallalar established the:

  • Sathya Dharma Salai
  • At Vadalur

Its purpose was to provide free food without caste discrimination.

The feeding centre was established during a period of severe famine and poverty.

Sathya Gnana Sabha

The Sathya Gnana Sabha was opened at Vadalur in:

  • 1872

Its central symbol was:

  • Divine light
  • Arutperunjothi

It differed from conventional temple worship through its emphasis on:

  • Formless divinity
  • Inner knowledge
  • Universal compassion
Thiruvarutpa

Vallalar’s devotional and philosophical songs were compiled as:

  • Thiruvarutpa
  • Songs of Grace

His teachings faced opposition from sections of Saiva orthodoxy.

Critics referred to his writings as:

  • Marutpa
Importance

Vallalar transformed religious devotion into an ethical programme centred on:

  • Hunger
  • Compassion
  • Equality
  • Non-violence
  • Service

Unlike some elite reform associations, his message reached broad Tamil-speaking communities.

Arumuga Navalar and Saiva Revival

Arumuga Navalar used printing, prose, schools and textual authority to defend and reorganise Saiva tradition against missionary criticism.

Identity

Arumuga Navalar lived from:

  • 1822 to 1879

He was born at:

  • Nallur in Jaffna

Although born in Sri Lanka, his educational, printing and religious activities strongly influenced Tamil Saiva communities in both Jaffna and Tamil Nadu.

Background

Christian missionary schools and publications criticised:

  • Saiva worship
  • Temple rituals
  • Hindu religious literature
  • Image worship

Navalar responded by using the same modern instruments employed by missionaries:

  • Schools
  • Printed books
  • Prose writing
  • Public sermons
  • Religious textbooks
Printing

Navalar became one of the earliest Tamil Saiva scholars to use printing systematically.

He edited and published:

  • Saiva texts
  • Classical Tamil works
  • Commentaries
  • Schoolbooks
  • Religious question-and-answer texts

His prose was direct and structured for students and general readers.

Education

He established:

  • Saiva Prakasa Vidyasala
  • Saiva schools based partly on modern classroom methods

He combined:

  • Tamil
  • Religious instruction
  • Secular subjects
  • Graded textbooks

A related school was established at Chidambaram during the 1860s.

Religious Reform

Navalar defended:

  • Saiva Siddhanta
  • Agamic temple worship
  • Tamil Saiva texts

He also criticised practices that he considered inconsistent with the Agamas.

His reform was therefore both:

  • A defence of tradition against missionary criticism
  • An attempt to regulate tradition through texts
Historical Caution

Navalar was a religious revivalist rather than an anti-caste reformer in the mould of Vaikundar, Vallalar or Iyothee Thass.

His primary contribution was:

  • Saiva revival
  • Tamil prose
  • Printing
  • Religious education

Detailed literary information belongs to Chapter 7.

Tamil Renaissance: Ellis, Caldwell and Dravidian Languages

Ellis and Caldwell established the intellectual basis for viewing Tamil and related South Indian languages as a family independent of Indo-Aryan.

Meaning of Tamil Renaissance

The Tamil Renaissance involved:

  • Rediscovery of ancient texts
  • Expansion of printing
  • Linguistic research
  • Historical study
  • Recovery of Tamil cultural traditions
  • New awareness of Tamil antiquity

It was both:

  • A literary development
  • A cultural and socio-political transformation
F. W. Ellis

F. W. Ellis lived from:

  • 1777 to 1819

Important associations:

  • College of Fort St. George
  • Study of South Indian languages
  • Recognition of a linguistic family separate from Indo-Aryan

In 1816, Ellis argued that the South Indian languages formed an independent family.

Robert Caldwell

Robert Caldwell lived from:

  • 1814 to 1891

His major work was:

  • A Comparative Grammar of the Dravidian or South-Indian Family of Languages
  • Published in 1856

Caldwell compared languages including:

  • Tamil
  • Telugu
  • Kannada
  • Malayalam

He popularised the term:

  • Dravidian language family
Social and Political Impact

The linguistic theory helped Tamil intellectuals argue that:

  • Tamil was not derived from Sanskrit
  • Tamil possessed an independent antiquity
  • South Indian cultures had a distinct historical development
  • Tamil identity could be separated from Sanskrit-centred narratives

These ideas later influenced:

  • Tamil cultural nationalism
  • Pure Tamil Movement
  • Non-Brahmin thought
  • Dravidian consciousness

However, detailed twentieth-century political use of these ideas belongs to Chapters 21, 23 and 25.

Historical Caution

Ellis formulated the basic separate-family argument before Caldwell.

Caldwell expanded and systematised it through comparative grammar.

Therefore:

  • Ellis — early formulation
  • Caldwell — systematic comparative development
Manuscript Recovery, Print Public Sphere and Tamil Identity

Manuscript recovery and print transformed classical Tamil texts into public cultural resources and helped create competing Saiva, secular, Buddhist, anti-caste and Dravidian interpretations of Tamil history.

Recovery of Classical Works

The nineteenth century witnessed major efforts to collect and publish palm-leaf manuscripts.

Important scholars included:

  • C. W. Damodaram Pillai
  • U. V. Swaminatha Iyer
  • Meenakshisundaram Pillai
  • Arumuga Navalar
C. W. Damodaram Pillai

Damodaram Pillai lived from:

  • 1832 to 1901

He collected, compared and edited manuscripts.

Important editions included:

  • Tolkappiyam
  • Virasoliyam
  • Iraiyanar Akapporul
  • Ilakkana Vilakkam
  • Kalithokai
  • Chulamani
U. V. Swaminatha Iyer

U. V. Swaminatha Iyer lived from:

  • 1855 to 1942

He was a student of:

  • Meenakshisundaram Pillai

Important nineteenth-century publications included:

  • Civaka Cintamani — 1887
  • Pattuppattu — 1889
  • Silappadikaram — 1892
  • Purananuru — 1894
  • Purapporul Venbamalai — 1895
  • Manimekalai — 1898

His twentieth-century publications belong to Chapter 7.

Impact on Society

Printed classical texts created awareness of:

  • Sangam society
  • Ancient Tamil rulers
  • Trade and ports
  • Tamil ethical traditions
  • Tamil grammatical antiquity
  • Jain and Buddhist contributions

The new print public sphere enabled debate through:

  • Newspapers
  • Journals
  • Public lectures
  • Associations
  • Textual commentaries
Cultural Self-Respect

The rediscovery of classical Tamil literature challenged the colonial idea that Tamil culture lacked an advanced past.

It also allowed later thinkers to construct competing interpretations of Tamil history:

  • Saiva
  • Secular
  • Buddhist
  • Anti-caste
  • Dravidian
  • Nationalist

Detailed author–work facts belong to Chapters 4–7. Here, the focus is their contribution to social identity.

Iyothee Thass: Anti-Caste Organisation and Education

Iyothee Thass linked anti-caste organisation, education, journalism and independent community representation during the late nineteenth century.

Early Life

Pandithar Iyothee Thass lived from:

  • 1845 to 1914

He was born in Madras and became known as:

  • Tamil scholar
  • Siddha medical practitioner
  • Linguist
  • Journalist
  • Anti-caste activist

He had knowledge of:

  • Tamil
  • English
  • Sanskrit
  • Pali
Opposition to Caste

Iyothee Thass criticised:

  • Untouchability
  • Caste hierarchy
  • Denial of education
  • Temple exclusion
  • Social humiliation
  • Brahmanical claims of authority

He argued that oppressed communities needed:

  • Education
  • Historical knowledge
  • Independent organisation
  • Control over their own identity
  • Access to print
Advaidananda Sabha

During the 1870s, he established the:

  • Advaidananda Sabha

Its activities addressed:

  • Social equality
  • Temple access
  • Education
  • Organisation of marginalised communities
Dravida Pandian

Iyothee Thass worked with:

  • Reverend John Rathinam

They were associated with the publication:

  • Dravida Pandian

The dates and exact organisational names vary between textbook and scholarly accounts. The publication belongs broadly to the 1880s anti-caste print movement.

Dravida Mahajana Sabha

Iyothee Thass established the:

  • Dravida Mahajana Sabha
  • In 1891

Its first major conference was held in:

  • The Nilgiris

Its demands included:

  • Education
  • Employment
  • Political representation
  • Removal of caste discrimination
  • Access to public institutions
Education

Iyothee Thass regarded education as essential for emancipation.

He supported schools for communities then officially described as:

  • Depressed Classes
  • Panchamas

His work helped marginalised groups enter a print sphere previously dominated by socially privileged communities.

Chapter Boundary

His weekly paper Oru Paisa Tamilan began in 1907.

It should be introduced here only as a continuation; its detailed twentieth-century role belongs to Chapter 21.

Iyothee Thass: Buddhism and Casteless Dravidian Identity

Iyothee Thass used Buddhism and casteless Dravidian identity to challenge the assumption that oppressed Tamil communities naturally belonged within Hindu caste society.

Rejection of Hindu Caste Identity

Iyothee Thass argued that oppressed Tamil communities should not identify themselves through a religion that legitimised their exclusion.

In the late nineteenth century, he urged them to identify as:

  • Casteless Dravidians
  • Sathi Petham Atra Dravidar

During census operations, he opposed their automatic classification as Hindus.

Journey to Sri Lanka

In 1898, Iyothee Thass travelled to Sri Lanka.

He received Buddhist initiation with the assistance of:

  • Colonel H. S. Olcott
  • Buddhist revivalist networks
Sakya Buddhist Society

In 1898, he founded the:

  • Sakya Buddhist Society
  • In Madras

It was also known through later organisational forms as the South Indian Buddhist Association.

Historical Interpretation

Iyothee Thass argued that:

  • Oppressed Tamil communities were originally Buddhists
  • Their history had been suppressed
  • Tamil literature contained traces of Buddhist ethics
  • Caste hierarchy was incompatible with Buddhist equality

He reinterpreted:

  • Tamil literature
  • Folk traditions
  • Religious history
  • Community identity

from a Buddhist and anti-caste perspective.

Buddhism as Emancipation

For Iyothee Thass, Buddhism represented:

  • Equality
  • Rational inquiry
  • Ethical conduct
  • Rejection of birth-based hierarchy
  • Recovery of lost identity

His Buddhist revival differed from purely spiritual revival because it was linked directly to:

  • Social justice
  • Community politics
  • Education
  • Historical reconstruction
Relationship to Rationalism

Iyothee Thass criticised superstition and caste-based religious authority.

However, the complete evolution of rationalist thought in Tamil Nadu belongs to Chapter 23.

Historical Importance

Iyothee Thass connected four major fields:

  • Anti-caste politics
  • Journalism
  • Tamil history
  • Buddhist revival

He created an intellectual tradition that later influenced Dalit, rationalist and Dravidian thought, though these later developments require separate treatment.

Rettamalai Srinivasan and the Paraiyar Mahajana Sabha

Rettamalai Srinivasan organised community demands through the Paraiyar Mahajana Sabha and the Paraiyan newspaper, deliberately turning a stigmatised name into a political identity.

Early Life

Rettamalai Srinivasan lived from:

  • Approximately 1859 or 1860 to 1945

The exact birth year varies across records.

He became an important:

  • Anti-caste organiser
  • Journalist
  • Community representative
  • Political activist
Paraiyar Mahajana Sabha

During the early 1890s, Srinivasan established the:

  • Paraiyar Mahajana Sabha

Different accounts use 1891, 1892 or 1893 for stages in its organisation and registration.

The association aimed to secure:

  • Education
  • Employment
  • Civil rights
  • Public access
  • Political representation
  • Recognition of community grievances
Paraiyan Newspaper

In October 1893, Srinivasan launched the Tamil newspaper:

  • Paraiyan

It publicised:

  • Untouchability
  • Educational discrimination
  • Employment exclusion
  • Public humiliation
  • Community demands
  • Government petitions

The title deliberately used a community name that was commonly employed as an insult.

Srinivasan sought to transform it into:

  • A public identity
  • A source of collective assertion
  • A political voice
Organised Representation

The Sabha submitted representations to:

  • Colonial authorities
  • Government officials
  • Public commissions

It helped create an organised political constituency among the oppressed communities of the Madras Presidency.

Difference from Iyothee Thass

Iyothee Thass generally rejected caste labels and promoted identities such as:

  • Casteless Dravidian
  • Buddhist
  • Original Tamil

Rettamalai Srinivasan initially used the term Paraiyar openly as a means of collective assertion.

Their strategies differed even though both challenged caste oppression.

Later Career

Srinivasan’s later activities included:

  • Legislative politics
  • Depressed Classes representation
  • Round Table Conferences
  • Collaboration and disagreement with other national leaders

These belong to Chapter 21 because they occurred mainly in the twentieth century.

From Social Reform to Political Representation

By the end of the nineteenth century, reform moved increasingly from religious centres and personal preaching to associations, print, conferences, petitions, census claims and formal political representation.

Transformation during the Century

At the beginning of the nineteenth century, many reforms were organised through:

  • Religious teachers
  • Missionaries
  • Local community leaders
  • Sacred centres

By the end of the century, movements increasingly used:

  • Registered associations
  • Newspapers
  • Public conferences
  • Petitions
  • Census categories
  • Government memoranda
  • Education statistics
  • Community representation
Major Changes
From Religious Reform to Social Organisation

Vaikundar and Vallalar used religious language to challenge:

  • Caste
  • Ritual hierarchy
  • Hunger
  • Social exclusion

Later organisations converted such grievances into:

  • Formal demands
  • Conferences
  • Written resolutions
From Manuscripts to Public Print

Printing allowed reformers to:

  • Reach readers beyond local centres
  • Debate opponents
  • Standardise arguments
  • Build collective identities
  • Record grievances
From Social Identity to Political Identity

Language, caste and community increasingly became the basis of political claims.

New identities included:

  • Tamil
  • Dravidian
  • Casteless Dravidian
  • Paraiyar
  • Buddhist
  • Non-Brahmin

These identities did not have identical meanings and should not be merged.

Foundations of Later Movements

Nineteenth-century developments prepared the ground for:

  • Non-Brahmin associations
  • Depressed Classes organisations
  • Labour movements
  • Justice Party
  • Rationalist movement
  • Self-Respect Movement
  • Dravidian Movement
Important Boundary

The following belong to later chapters:

  • Madras Non-Brahmin Association — 1909
  • Madras United League — 1912
  • Dravidian Association
  • Dravidian Home — 1916
  • South Indian Liberal Federation — 1916
  • Non-Brahmin Manifesto — 1916
  • Justice Party government — from 1920
  • Self-Respect Movement — from 1925

Chapter 20 explains the nineteenth-century foundations, not the detailed operation of these later organisations.

Rapid Revision and High-Yield Distinctions

The final topic consolidates chronology, reformer–place, organisation and publication associations and the distinctions needed to separate similar movements and identity strategies.

Essential Chronology
  • 1578 — Thambiran Vanakkam printed
  • 1709 — Ziegenbalg’s full-fledged press at Tranquebar
  • 1809 — Birth of Ayya Vaikundar
  • 1812 — Early printed edition of Thirukkural
  • 1816 — Ellis formulated the separate South Indian language-family argument
  • 1822–1859 — Major phase of the Upper Cloth Movement
  • 1823 — Birth of Vallalar
  • 1833 — Vaikundar’s meditation at Samithoppu
  • 1845 — Birth of Iyothee Thass
  • 1851 — Death of Ayya Vaikundar
  • 1856 — Caldwell’s Comparative Grammar
  • 1856 — Hindu Widows’ Remarriage Act
  • 1859 — Travancore Upper Cloth proclamation
  • 1859/1860 — Birth of Rettamalai Srinivasan
  • 1864 — Veda Samaj established in Madras
  • 1865 — Vallalar established Samarasa Vedha Sanmarga Sangam
  • 1867 — Sathya Dharma Salai established at Vadalur
  • 1872 — Sathya Gnana Sabha opened
  • 1874 — Death of Vallalar
  • 1875 — Theosophical Society founded
  • 1879 — Death of Arumuga Navalar
  • 1882 — Theosophical headquarters established at Adyar
  • 1887 — Civaka Cintamani published by U. V. Swaminatha Iyer
  • 1889 — Pattuppattu published
  • 1891 — Dravida Mahajana Sabha
  • 1891 — Age of Consent raised to twelve
  • 1892 — Silappadikaram published
  • 1893 — Paraiyan newspaper launched
  • 1894 — Purananuru published
  • 1897 — Ramakrishna Math established in Madras
  • 1898 — Iyothee Thass embraced Buddhism and founded the Sakya Buddhist Society
  • 1898 — Manimekalai published
Reformer–Place Associations
  • Ayya Vaikundar — Samithoppu
  • Vallalar — Marudhur and Vadalur
  • Arumuga Navalar — Nallur, Jaffna and Chidambaram
  • Theosophical Society — Adyar
  • Ramakrishna Math — Ice House, Madras
  • Iyothee Thass — Madras and Nilgiris
  • Rettamalai Srinivasan — Madras Presidency
  • Upper Cloth Movement — South Travancore and present Kanyakumari region
Reformer–Organisation Associations
  • Ayya Vaikundar — Samathuva Samajam
  • Vallalar — Samarasa Suddha Sanmarga Sathya Sangam
  • K. Sridharalu Naidu — Veda Samaj
  • Blavatsky and Olcott — Theosophical Society
  • Swami Ramakrishnananda — Ramakrishna Math, Madras
  • Iyothee Thass — Advaidananda Sabha and Dravida Mahajana Sabha
  • Iyothee Thass — Sakya Buddhist Society
  • Rettamalai Srinivasan — Paraiyar Mahajana Sabha
Reformer–Publication Associations
  • Vallalar — Thiruvarutpa
  • Ayya Vaikundar — Akilathirattu Ammanai tradition
  • Caldwell — Comparative Grammar
  • Iyothee Thass and John Rathinam — Dravida Pandian
  • Rettamalai Srinivasan — Paraiyan
  • U. V. Swaminatha Iyer — Civaka Cintamani, Pattuppattu, Silappadikaram, Purananuru and Manimekalai
High-Yield Distinctions
Reformist versus Revivalist Movement

Reformist

  • Altered existing religious and social practices
  • Criticised ritual and caste
  • Example: Veda Samaj

Revivalist

  • Defended or renewed religious tradition
  • Used selected ancient texts as authority
  • Example: Arumuga Navalar’s Saiva revival
Ayya Vaikundar versus Vallalar

Ayya Vaikundar

  • South Travancore
  • Ayyavazhi
  • Samathuva Samajam
  • Turban, inter-dining and social dignity
  • Direct criticism of political and caste authority

Vallalar

  • Vadalur
  • Sanmarga movement
  • Jeevakarunyam
  • Sathya Dharma Salai
  • Compassion and feeding the hungry
Veda Samaj versus Theosophical Society

Veda Samaj

  • Founded in Madras in 1864
  • Influenced by Brahmo Samaj
  • Monotheism and social reform

Theosophical Society

  • Founded in New York in 1875
  • Headquarters moved to Adyar in 1882
  • Comparative religion and universal brotherhood
Theosophical Society versus Ramakrishna Math

Theosophical Society

  • Blavatsky and Olcott
  • Adyar
  • Comparative religious study

Ramakrishna Math

  • Swami Ramakrishnananda
  • Madras, 1897
  • Vedanta and service
Ellis versus Caldwell

Ellis

  • 1816
  • Early formulation of a separate South Indian language family

Caldwell

  • 1856
  • Comparative Grammar
  • Systematic use of the term Dravidian family
Damodaram Pillai versus U. V. Swaminatha Iyer

Damodaram Pillai

  • Edited grammar and literary manuscripts
  • Tolkappiyam, Kalithokai and other texts

U. V. Swaminatha Iyer

  • Recovered and published major classical literary works
  • Pattuppattu, Silappadikaram, Purananuru and Manimekalai
Iyothee Thass versus Rettamalai Srinivasan

Iyothee Thass

  • Casteless Dravidian identity
  • Buddhist revival
  • Rejection of Hindu caste identity
  • Dravida Mahajana Sabha

Rettamalai Srinivasan

  • Paraiyar identity used for political assertion
  • Paraiyar Mahajana Sabha
  • Paraiyan newspaper
Upper Cloth Movement versus Women’s Education Movement

Upper Cloth Movement

  • Dress and bodily dignity
  • Nadar women
  • South Travancore
  • Major proclamation in 1859

Women’s education

  • Literacy and schooling
  • Missionary and reform-association support
  • Broader Madras Presidency debate
Tamil Renaissance versus Pure Tamil Movement

Tamil Renaissance

  • Nineteenth-century recovery of classical Tamil
  • Manuscript publication
  • Linguistic research
  • Cultural identity

Pure Tamil Movement

  • Mainly twentieth-century organised movement
  • Removal of Sanskrit influence
  • Detailed treatment belongs to Chapter 21
Exam Traps
  • The Upper Cloth Movement occurred in Travancore, not directly under ordinary Madras Presidency administration.
  • Present Kanyakumari district formed part of South Travancore during the movement.
  • Ayya Vaikundar founded Samathuva Samajam.
  • Vallalar founded Samarasa Vedha Sanmarga Sangam.
  • Sathya Dharma Salai was established at Vadalur in 1867.
  • Sathya Gnana Sabha is associated with 1872.
  • Veda Samaj was founded in Madras in 1864.
  • Theosophical Society headquarters moved to Adyar in 1882.
  • Ramakrishna Math in Madras began in 1897.
  • Ellis presented the separate-language-family argument before Caldwell.
  • Caldwell’s Comparative Grammar was published in 1856.
  • Iyothee Thass founded Dravida Mahajana Sabha in 1891.
  • Iyothee Thass founded the Sakya Buddhist Society in 1898.
  • Rettamalai Srinivasan launched Paraiyan in 1893.
  • Iyothee Thass and Rettamalai Srinivasan used different identity strategies.
  • Justice Party belongs to Chapter 22, not Chapter 20.
  • Detailed rationalism belongs to Chapter 23.
  • Self-Respect Movement belongs to Chapters 24 and 26.
  • Detailed Dravidian Movement belongs to Chapters 25 and 27.
